source: Straubinger, Kreis, Lukasczyk, Fraser (2025) Mutation Testing via Iterative LLM-Driven Scientific Debugging
finding: Closest ablation of the hypothesis/prediction/experiment loop found. Scientific-debugging prompts (hypothesis with predicted result, experiment, conclusion) were compared with plain iterative retry that has no hypotheses. Both iterate and do about equally well. The scientific prompt costs much more.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini, Python projects, up to 1,000 mutants per project. Baseline (one shot): branch coverage ~55%, mutation score ~60%, success clearly lowest (p<0.001). Iterative (no hypotheses), Scientific 0-shot and 1-shot: branch coverage ~80%, line ~90%, mutation score ~80%, success near 60%, about 4,000 tests each. Scientific variants used significantly more tokens and cost.
quote: The specific way the LLM is prompted matters less, as long as the process is iterative
limits: Task is writing tests that kill a mutant, not fixing a bug. One small model. The prediction is bundled with the hypothesis, so it cannot isolate the prediction step.
agent_relevance: Evidence against assuming the structured loop beats plain retry at equal success. It buys explanations, not accuracy, and costs tokens. Any predict step should be tested at equal tokens.

source: Straubinger et al. (2025), RQ3 equivalence claims
finding: The hypothesis-style prompts declared many mutants 'equivalent' (unkillable). Many of those were later killed by other tests. So an abandoned hypothesis was often a failed search, not a true negative.
numbers: Both scientific variants flagged over 15% of mutants as equivalent; Baseline flagged none; Iterative a small number. Manual review found many flagged mutants were in fact killable, mostly by other LLM-generated tests.
limits: Equivalence is a different judgement from bug refutation. Some sample counts in the extracted text were truncated, so none are quoted.
agent_relevance: A confident 'cannot be done / hypothesis refuted' verdict from the model is unreliable. Check that the probe really ran and tried a different input before accepting a refutation.

source: Ma et al. (2025/2026) DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
finding: Turns failure-attribution hypotheses into interventions and re-runs. Most hypotheses end Inconclusive, mainly because the agent system did not carry out the intervention. This is a second count of invalid experiments (gap 3), in a multi-agent setting rather than code.
numbers: Intervened trials 72 (WW-AB), 99 (WW-GAIA), 63 (GAIA-Level-1). Validated 15.3 / 16.2 / 34.9%. Refuted 13.9 / 21.2 / 23.8%. Partially validated 4.2 / 5.1 / 12.7%. Inconclusive 66.7 / 57.6 / 28.6%. Each trial run 3 times.
limits: Domain is agent trajectories, not program bugs. Whether an intervention was 'fulfilled' is judged by an LLM (GPT-5), so labels are model output. Executor GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: About 60% of experiments on hard cases told us nothing because they were not carried out. A predict-observe check needs an explicit 'did the probe execute as planned' flag, so no-ops are not scored as refutations.

source: Ma et al. (2025/2026) DoVer, ground-truth analysis
finding: Log-based blame (which step caused the failure) is itself an unverified hypothesis. Accuracy is low and depends on whether the true cause is unambiguous.
numbers: 29 GAIA cases from Who&When: 14 judged to have uncertain ground truth. Step accuracy on uncertain cases: GPT-4o 24%, GPT-5 7%. On the 15 certain cases: GPT-4o 44%, GPT-5 53%. GPT-4o all-at-once step accuracy rose from 6% to 24% after prompt fixes.
limits: Small n (29 cases). Authors' own re-annotation.
agent_relevance: Hypotheses made from reading a log, with no run, are right well under half the time. Support for forcing a test before acting on a blame claim.

source: Ma et al. (2025/2026) DoVer, failure flipping and model strength
finding: Testing hypotheses by intervention flips some failures to success. The gain is modest and depends on the debugging model.
numbers: Trial success rate 17.6% (WW), 27.5% (GAIA-Level-1), about 49.0% (GSMPlus). Progress made about +8.8% / +15.7% in two settings and near +0% in WW-AB. A small open model as debugger: 11.3% trial success zero-shot, 14.3% with a 3-shot prompt, versus 17.6% with GPT-4o.
limits: Comparators are Self-Refine and CRITIC style; no human baseline. LLM-judged progress.
agent_relevance: Verifying hypotheses by action recovers about 10 to 30 percent of failures in this setting, and weaker debugging models lose a third or more of it.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym (re-read of the SWE-bench-Lite table and prose)
finding: Rewrite-only agent vs debug (pdb from the start) vs debug(5) (pdb after the 5th rewrite). The debugger helps strong reasoning models and hurts or does nothing for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. The Llama-3.3-70B row goes up in the table, but the prose lists Llama among models that are harmed. Table and prose disagree.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite (300 tasks), mean +/- sd of 3 runs, rewrite / debug / debug(5): GPT-4o 19.1/17.2/23.6; GPT-4o-mini 4.0/3.5/6.2; o1-preview 10.7/30.2/30.8; o3-mini 8.5/22.1/19.8; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 37.2/48.4/52.1; Llama-3.3-70B 2.4/4.0/4.8 (sd 0.5/1.0/0.4).
quote: accessing the pdb tool at the beginning ... could to some extent harm the overall performance
limits: Minimal prompt-based agents; the authors call them demonstrations. Llama base rate 2.4% so +1.6 is near noise. Not a clean strength ordering: o1-preview rewrite (10.7) is below GPT-4o (19.1) yet gains most from pdb.
agent_relevance: Crossover is not set by general strength alone. Strongest rows gain 10 to 20 points from pdb. Delayed access (debug(5)) did not fall below rewrite in any row, so a late-probe policy is the safe default.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym, Mini-nightmare (10 hand-made bugs)
finding: On short hand-made buggy programs the debugger adds little for most models because the code and the test failure are enough. Reasoning models are already near ceiling.
numbers: Closed-weights success % rewrite / debug / debug(5): GPT-4o 40.0/40.0/53.3; GPT-4o-mini 13.3/6.7/16.7; o1-preview 100/100/100; o3-mini 100/96.7/100; Claude 3.7 93.3/96.7/93.3. Three runs, ten tasks. Open-weights panel layout was not clean in the text, so not quoted.
agent_relevance: Probe access cannot be tested on easy bugs. Needs bugs where the test failure does not point to the cause.

source: Garg and Huang (2026) Debug2Fix: Can Interactive Debugging Help Coding Agents Fix More Bugs?
finding: Most recent test of debugger access with frontier models (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5). A debug subagent that answers runtime questions raised pass rate on GitBug-Java and SWE-Bench-Live. Exposing raw debugger tools to the main agent did not help.
numbers: GitBug-Java pass rate: GPT-5 60.2 to 73.1 (+21.8% relative) with Debug2Fix plus tool limit (edits blocked until the subagent is called once); Claude Sonnet +13% relative; Haiku +16% relative. Debug-tools-only: flat for GPT-5 and Haiku, Sonnet 64.5 (-14.8%). SWE-Bench-Live: GPT-5 gain 16%, Haiku 12%, Sonnet minimal.
limits: One group (Microsoft), no independent replication. Gains are relative to the authors' own baseline. The subagent adds steps and tokens (Sonnet: about 33 subagent steps and 400k tokens on GitBug-Java). SWE-Bench-Live absolute numbers could not be read cleanly from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Probe access helps strong 2025 models when wrapped as a question-and-answer step the model must call before editing. That is close to a forced predict-observe step.

source: Garg and Huang (2026) Debug2Fix, ablation and adoption
finding: Models under-use a debugger when it is optional. Claude Sonnet 4.5 called the subagent in only 8% of SWE-Bench-Live instances and gained little. With raw debug tools in Java it did better when it used them, but it used them in only 9% of instances.
numbers: Natural call rate 60-70% in Java; about 99% when edits are blocked until a debug call. SWE-Bench-Live call rate: GPT-5 above 60%, Haiku 33.2%, Sonnet 8%. Sonnet with raw tools: used a debug tool in 17 instances (9%); resolved 14 (82%) vs 11 (64%) for the same instances in baseline. Debug sequences averaged 4 tool calls.
limits: Selection effect: the 17 instances chose to use the tool. 17 is a tiny n.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly answered. The issue is not only model strength but whether the model chooses to probe. A hard gate (no edit before an observation) fixes the under-use.

source: Chen et al. (2024/2025) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: Tests whether models predict coverage, program state, execution path and output of HumanEval and ClassEval programs, and whether those answers agree with each other (Incremental Consistency, IC). Output prediction is easiest. Intermediate steps are worse and often disagree with the final answer.
numbers: 15 models. Mean accuracy on runtime behavior reasoning 44.4%, mean IC score 10.3. GPT-4-Turbo best: 75.0% average accuracy, IC 42.5 (other models more than 21.9 IC points lower). Output prediction above 50% for all models; only about half of models (8 of 15) were above 50% on some of the other tasks.
limits: 2023-era models. Functions from HumanEval and ClassEval, not repository bugs. Does not link prediction error to a wrong fix.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 only partly closed. Strong models predict intermediate state worse than final output and the two often disagree. A predict-then-observe check should store the predicted state, not just the output.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) LDB: Debug like a Human, verifying runtime execution step by step
finding: Compares real runtime traces (variable values per basic block) with the model simulating the run itself (Self-Debug Expl and Trace). Real traces give steadier gains. Model-simulated traces added nothing on the weakest model, and the authors say wrong self-predictions can misguide debugging.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1 (GPT-3.5): baseline 73.8, SD 81.1 and 80.5, LDB 82.9. StarCoder row: 39.0 baseline, SD 38.4 (-0.6) and 39.0 (+0.0), LDB 39.6. Stronger seed programs: GPT-4 seed 87.2 to 89.6 with LDB (+2.4), Reflexion seed 91.5 to 95.1 (+3.6). SD curves plateau after 2-3 rounds while LDB keeps rising.
quote: LLMs are prone to mistakes when reflecting on program execution
limits: Debugger backbone is GPT-3.5 in the main tables; needs visible tests; function-level tasks; authors' own framework.
agent_relevance: Direct sign that a wrong pre-run prediction can hurt and that real observation, not self-simulation, drives the gain. The gain shrinks as the seed program gets better (+9.1 to +2.4).

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2023) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug
finding: Rubber-duck style code explanation gives small gains without tests. With unit tests the gain is larger because execution supplies a real signal. Correct/wrong feedback alone does not help when no test exists.
numbers: Text-to-SQL (Spider) with code explanation: +2 to +3 points, +9 points on the hardest problems. With unit tests (TransCoder, MBPP): up to +12 points. Simple feedback on Spider: no notable gain because the model cannot tell right from wrong SQL.
limits: Old models (Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 at the time). Small ablations.
agent_relevance: Cross-check on d11: the gain comes from the external run, not from the model's own judgement of correctness. The model's own verdict alone is not a trustworthy signal.

source: Spiess et al. (2024) Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code
finding: Model confidence in generated code (including program repair) is poorly calibrated out of the box. Rescaling with known labels helps. Asking the model to reflect gives inconsistent gains.
numbers: Expected Calibration Error 0.09 to 0.73 across tasks (synthesis, line completion, repair) and models (GPT-3.5, Codex, CodeGen2-16B). Few-shot reflective GPT-3.5 completion raised the Brier skill score from 0 to 0.15.
limits: 2023-era models, temperature 0. Not a DONE-token study. Not tested on current reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open for 2025 models. The older evidence says do not use the model's own confidence as a stop rule without calibration on labelled cases or an external check.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) Can We Predict Before Executing Machine Learning Agents? (ForeAgent)
finding: Tests LLM prediction in place of execution. Pairwise prediction of which of two ML solutions scores better is only moderately above chance. An agent that predicts, then verifies the few chosen candidates, converges faster.
numbers: 18,438 pairs. DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 61.5%, GPT-5.1 58.8% (chance 50.0%, complexity heuristic 50.8%). Thinking mode 61.3% vs direct answer 55.9%. Listwise Accuracy@1 falls from 61.3% to 31.1%. Validation-metric proxy alone: 72.2%. ForeAgent: about 6x faster convergence and about +6% over the execution-based AIDE baseline on MLE-bench AI4Science tasks.
limits: Predicts which solution wins, not what a probe prints. ML domain. The same group built the dataset and the agent. Calibration is shown in a figure only.
agent_relevance: Predictions are only mildly better than chance, yet gating execution on them still saved time. Treat a prediction as a cheap filter that must still be checked by running.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: A Debugging Interface for Asking Questions About Program Behavior (CHI)
finding: Primary source for Whyline-style why did and why didn't questions. PDF read. Small user test on Alice with participants from a Masters HCI program.
numbers: Formative studies: 50% of all errors came from false assumptions in hypotheses formed while debugging; 68% of programmer questions were why didn't. Test: 4 users With Whyline vs 4 Without, 90 minutes. Tasks completed M=3.20 (SD .457) vs M=2.25 (SD .500), t(7)=3.0, p<.02 (40% increase). Debug time in 6 matching scenarios cut by a factor of 7.8 on average, F(1,5)=12.64, p<.02. Whyline useful for 19 of 24 questions.
limits: Eight participants. Alice, a novice environment. The time analysis is over six scenarios, not over people. Only the authors tested it. The 2008 Java version was not opened.
agent_relevance: The 7.8x is a six-scenario mean among 8 people. Soften any claim. The why-didn't form (ask why the expected thing did not happen) was the part users valued most.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: Evaluating Debugging Capability of LLMs
finding: Re-opened for the bug-type question. Runtime feedback helped syntax and reference errors, and was unhelpful or disruptive for logic errors. Logic and multiple-bug cases are harder.
numbers: 4,253 instances, 18 bug types, four categories (syntax, reference, logic, multiple). GPT-4-0613 passes 75.0%, GPT-3.5-0613 62.1% overall. Models take under 10 s per bug vs about 20 min for humans. Effect sizes by bug type are only in Figure 4 and could not be read as numbers.
quote: for logic bugs, the details provided in traceback messages are often too low-level
limits: Bugs inserted by GPT-4 into LeetCode solutions, single functions. Runtime feedback means traceback or test output, not a hypothesis-driven probe.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partly closed. For logic bugs raw error output misleads, so the agent needs a model of expected behaviour (a prediction) to interpret it. Not tested directly.
